tldr: The authors developed "LocoPilot," a teleoperation framework that allows a single human operator to intuitively command both a quadruped robot and a manipulator simultaneously while receiving haptic force feedback for imitation learning data collection. By sharing the exact same 11-dimensional action interface between data collection and autonomous deployment, they achieved real-robot deployment of a VLA model (MolmoAct2) without action retargeting.
hero_caption: Overall view of the LocoPilot teleoperation setup. At the leader station on the left, a Nintendo Joy-Con is mounted to the end of a Piper L arm sharing the same degrees of freedom, allowing the right hand to command arm posture, torso pitch, yaw rate, and the gripper, while the left hand controls base translation velocity. Commands are sent in real time to the follower physical robot on the right (quadruped + arm + wrist camera) while providing force feedback to the operator.
overview:
Legged loco-manipulation—mounting a manipulator on a quadruped robot—is a dream configuration capable of moving and performing tasks freely over uneven terrain. However, collecting the high-quality demonstrations required for imitation learning has been a major barrier. While robot-free setups using handheld sensors (such as UMI) are convenient, they cannot capture robot-specific information such as legged locomotion dynamics or on-board camera shake, requiring complex retargeting to the physical platform. On the other hand, directly teleoperating the physical robot makes it extremely difficult for a single operator to coordinate base movement and the arm's many degrees of freedom, often resulting in disjointed, sequential motions such as "walk, stop, then move the arm."

To solve this challenge, the authors built "LocoPilot," a bilateral teleoperation system that enables a single operator to concurrently control base translation, body pitch, 6-DoF arm motion, and the gripper. By moving the leader arm with the dominant hand while operating the sticks and triggers of a compact controller mounted to its grip, and holding a second controller in the other hand, the operator can achieve smooth, simultaneous coordinated motions. Furthermore, the system incorporates a mechanism to estimate external contact forces and render haptic feedback to the leader arm without expensive torque sensors, alongside a unified 11-dimensional action space shared identically between collection and autonomous deployment.

In physical experiments using a Unitree Go2 and a Piper L arm, the authors confirmed stable teleoperation while grasping and pushing a 1.5 kg payload. Furthermore, by fine-tuning MolmoAct2, a large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, on 289 collected demonstration episodes, they successfully reproduced smooth, autonomous mobile pick-and-place behaviors directly on the physical robot without any additional inverse kinematics calculations or action retargeting.
contributions: Built bilateral teleoperation hardware and software enabling a single operator to fully coordinate base translation, torso pitch, 6-DoF arm motion, and gripper opening/closing simultaneously.

Implemented a framework to estimate contact forces from generalized momentum residuals without dedicated force/torque sensors, safely feeding force feedback back to the operator via passivity control (energy tanks).

Realized a pipeline that shares a unified 11D action representation (base planar velocity, yaw rate, pitch angle, 6 arm joint angles, and gripper state) between data collection and autonomous policy deployment, integrated directly with downstream locomotion and arm control stacks.
Demonstrated autonomous physical deployment of legged loco-manipulation by fine-tuning an open VLA model (MolmoAct2) on collected demonstrations without action retargeting.

sections.heading: The Barriers of Concurrent Control and the Deployment Gap in Legged Manipulation Demonstrations
sections.summary: Training legged mobile manipulators requires demonstration data where legged locomotion and arm motion are smoothly coordinated. However, existing handheld sensor approaches miss platform-specific dynamics, while conventional physical teleoperation makes it extremely difficult for a single operator to control all degrees of freedom at once.
sections.details:
Unlike fixed-base manipulators, mounting an arm onto a quadruped robot offers an infinite workspace, but it demands smooth, whole-body coordination such as reaching out while walking or pitching the torso forward to grasp distant objects. Recently, the trend of applying large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to robot imitation learning has gained rapid momentum. Yet in legged loco-manipulation, collecting coordinated whole-body motions directly on target physical platforms has remained a major unsolved challenge.

Existing demonstration collection methods come with trade-offs. For instance, robot-free approaches using handheld grippers like UMI (Universal Manipulation Interface) are accessible and intuitive. However, they do not record legged locomotion gaits, body-mounted camera shakes, or proprioception, necessitating complex retargeting when deploying learned policies onto physical robots. In contrast, on-robot teleoperation captures platform-specific signals directly, but having a single human concurrently control both base movement and arm degrees of freedom is remarkably difficult. Prior work has often relied on multiple operators sharing roles or partial automation, which can lead to fragmented behaviors or fail to directly capture operator intent.

LocoPilot tackles these challenges from two directions. First, it introduces a bilateral teleoperation interface enabling a single operator to simultaneously command base translation, torso pitch, the arm, and the gripper. Second, it utilizes the exact same 11-dimensional action interface and control stack during both data collection and autonomous deployment, eliminating any retargeting gap.

sections.heading: Hardware and Software: Intuitive Coordinated Control Using Both Hands
sections.summary: The follower physical platform utilizes a Unitree Go2, an AgileX Piper L arm, and two RealSense cameras. At the leader station, a Nintendo Joy-Con is mounted to the end of a second Piper L arm, allowing the right hand to control the arm, pitch, yaw, and gripper, while the left hand commands base translation using a second Joy-Con.
sections.details:
### II-A Hardware
The follower physical robot consists of a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped robot carrying a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L arm and a parallel gripper on its back. For visual sensing, an Intel RealSense D435 is mounted near the gripper for close-up manipulation, and an Intel RealSense D405 with a wide field of view is placed on the robot's head.

At the leader station used for data collection, another Piper L arm with the same kinematic structure as the follower serves as the leader device. The key design here is the integration of a Nintendo Joy-Con directly onto the leader arm's end-effector handle. The operator grasps this handle with their dominant (right) hand to move the leader arm directly through space, using the thumb analog stick to command torso pitch and yaw rate, and the index finger trigger to actuate the gripper. Simultaneously, the other (left) hand holds a second Joy-Con to provide forward, backward, and lateral base translation velocities. This enables a single human to naturally coordinate whole-body motion. On the visual side, video streams from the on-board cameras are displayed in real time, ensuring the operator shares the exact viewpoint of the policy model.

### II-B Software Architecture
The software is built on ROS 2 Jazzy and Cyclone DDS. On the follower robot, an RL-based locomotion policy, a MUSE state estimator, an arm control stack, and camera streaming nodes run concurrently. The robot-side software modules remain completely identical between teleoperated data collection and autonomous operation. The only difference is who provides the 11-dimensional action command: during collection, it originates from the operator's leader station; during autonomous deployment, it comes from the policy inference node. Because downstream interfaces are standardized, the architecture is modular and allows easy replacement of the locomotion controller or arm controller with alternative hardware.

captions.F2: Hardware configuration of the teleoperation system. At the leader station on the left, a Joy-Con is mounted on a custom handle at the end of the Piper L arm, enabling one hand to control arm posture alongside buttons and analog sticks. On the right, the physical follower robot mounts an identical Piper L arm and wrist RGB-D camera on the quadruped.

sections.heading: Sensorless Force Rendering and a Unified 11D Action Interface
sections.summary: Contact forces are estimated via a momentum residual observer without dedicated force sensors, and haptic feedback is rendered safely using energy-tank-based passivity control. Data collection and policy deployment are directly linked through a shared 11D action representation (base velocities, pitch, arm joint angles, and gripper).
sections.details:
### III-A Leader-Follower Arm Mapping
Because the leader and follower share identical joint configurations, direct mapping in joint space is employed. The follower faithfully tracks the leader's joint positions using PD control with gravity compensation.

For the force feedback channel, rather than mounting an expensive and heavy force/torque sensor at the follower tip, an online generalized-momentum residual filter estimates external joint torques $\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext}}$. The estimated residual torque $\mathbf{r}$ passes through a low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of $f_c = 5\text{ Hz}$, and the low-frequency contact force information is rendered back to the operator's hand via the leader actuators. Consistent with prior findings, rendering low-frequency contact components alone significantly improves execution time and operator control effort.

To address system stability issues inherent to bilateral teleoperation, a passivity layer restricted to the operator-side port was introduced. Energy dissipated by damping on the leader side is stored in a virtual energy tank $H$. Commanded torques are scaled so that the power injected into the system by force rendering never exceeds the remaining tank energy. This mathematically guarantees passivity, preventing instability despite environmental or model uncertainties.

### III-B Unified Loco-Manipulation and Learning Interface
Operator inputs and autonomous policy outputs are unified into the following 11-dimensional vector:
$$\mathbf{a} = [v_x^d, v_y^d, \omega_z^d, \theta^d, \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{arm}}^{d\top}, g^d]^\top$$
Here, $v_x^d, v_y^d$ are desired base planar translation velocities, $\omega_z^d$ is desired yaw rate, $\theta^d$ is desired absolute torso pitch, $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{arm}}^d \in \mathbb{R}^6$ represents arm joint target angles, and $g^d$ is the gripper opening state.

For base locomotion control, an RL policy based on BinWalker is employed. To handle center-of-mass shifts and reaction forces when reaching far forward, arm joint angles $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{arm}}$ are included in the locomotion policy's proprioceptive observations, and the domain randomization range during training was expanded. Collected data is synchronously logged in the LeRobot format, directly recording camera frames, proprioception, and the actual 11D commands received by the robot, making it immediately ready for policy training without post-processing.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Accurate Force Tracking and Autonomous Pick-and-Place with a VLA Model
sections.summary: Teleoperation experiments using a known 1.5 kg payload quantitatively evaluated position tracking and external force estimation accuracy. Furthermore, MolmoAct2 was fine-tuned on 289 collected demonstrations, successfully achieving autonomous, language-conditioned mobile pick-and-place tasks on the physical robot.
sections.details:
### IV-A Arm-to-arm Teleoperation
The authors verified tracking and force estimation performance through a tabletop pick-and-place task using a calibrated 1.5 kg weight (approx. 14.7 N gravitational force). In free space, the mean end-effector position tracking error was 8.02 mm, and the force estimation noise floor (RMSE) was 1.27 N. During lifting and carrying phases, the vertical force estimation error stayed within an RMSE of 2.25 N (15.3% of the true value), confirming that environmental contact and load magnitude were reliably conveyed to the operator's hands.

### IV-B VLA Deployment
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the collected demonstrations, the open-weight 5.5-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action model MolmoAct2 was fine-tuned. Two task types were targeted: "Grasp," where the robot approaches, grasps, and carries a cube located beyond arm reach from its initial position to a target area, and "Push," where the robot pushes it to the target. Using red or white cubes, a total of 289 episodes (259 Grasp, 30 Push) were collected.

The VLA backbone was adapted using LoRA (rank 512), while the action head was fully trained across all parameters. When deployed on the physical robot, the model received natural language instructions such as "Move the red cube to the blue square" and directly outputted 11D actions from two camera streams and proprioception. The robot autonomously walked toward the target, pitched its torso forward to extend the arm's reachable workspace, grasped the cube, transported it to the goal, and released it—performing smooth base-arm coordination in a single unified sequence. Even when the target drifted out of view or stopping positions misaligned, adaptive retry behaviors such as repushing or re-grasping were observed.

captions.F4: Experimental data while grasping and carrying a 1.5 kg payload. (a) End-effector position error $\|\mathbf{e}\|$ and (b) estimated vertical force $|F_z|$ over time. During free motion (blue background), force estimation stays close to zero (1.27 N noise floor), while during the grasping and carrying phase (red background), forces are estimated accurately near the theoretical payload value (dashed line).
captions.F5: Autonomous real-robot deployment of fine-tuned MolmoAct2. Given the prompt "Move the red cube to the blue square," the robot autonomously executes the full sequence: (a, b) base walking approach, (c) torso pitching forward while reaching to grasp, (d, e) turning and carrying the cube to the goal, and (f) accurately releasing it.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Challenges: Floating-Base Inertia and Task Suitability
sections.summary: Because the contact force estimation model assumes a fixed base, rapid base acceleration can cause inertial forces to be falsely detected as external contacts. Additionally, the autonomous policy evaluation remains qualitative, leaving quantitative analyses of dataset scaling and success rates for future work.
sections.details:
The authors frankly discuss the limitations and applicability of their system. First, the momentum residual observer for contact force estimation relies on the dynamic model of the manipulator alone, treating the quadruped base as an inertial reference frame (a static base). Consequently, rapid accelerations or sharp turns by the base introduce inertial forces at the arm joints, which are misestimated as external contact forces. Furthermore, unmodeled dynamics such as joint drive stiction introduce biases, forming a noise floor of approximately 1.27 N. Mitigating this will require incorporating inertial force compensation using estimated base accelerations.

In addition, the force rendering channel provides the greatest utility in tasks where sustained contact constraints occur outside camera view, such as opening doors, turning valves, or pushing/pulling heavy objects. Conversely, for tasks dominated by free-space locomotion or brief, light contacts, the relative contribution of force feedback is smaller.

Finally, the evaluation of autonomous deployment remains qualitative across a single robot embodiment and a limited number of trials. Quantitative scaling analyses connecting demonstration volume to task success rates, as well as ablation studies evaluating the direct impact of haptic feedback on human demonstration quality, remain open challenges.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Foundation for Mobile Manipulation Bridging the Gap Between Real Robots and Learning
sections.summary: LocoPilot establishes a framework for single-operator whole-body coordinated teleoperation and provides an identical 11D action space from data collection to policy deployment. Validated end-to-end through physical VLA deployment, it is expected to serve as a standard foundation for future legged loco-manipulation learning.
sections.details:
This paper presented LocoPilot, an integrated teleoperation and data-collection framework for legged mobile manipulators. It achieves a bilateral interface where a single human can concurrently command base translation, torso pitch, arm joints, and the gripper, incorporating sensorless contact force estimation and passivity-guaranteed force feedback.

The framework's greatest strength is that the commands input by the human during teleoperation and those output by the trained policy during autonomous deployment are designed around the exact same 11-dimensional action representation (and identical downstream controllers). This completely eliminates any need for translation or retargeting between demonstration collection, policy training, and real-robot deployment. The successful physical deployment of the open-source VLA model MolmoAct2 clearly illustrates the practical utility of this pipeline. As adding new tasks and data within this framework is straightforward, it is expected to serve as a powerful data collection foundation toward realizing embodied generalist AI agents.

takeaways: Matching operator inputs during data collection with policy outputs at deployment—across both the action space and the control stack—completely removes distribution shift and additional IK calculations caused by retargeting.

Integrating off-the-shelf controllers directly onto the leader arm's handle enables a single operator to achieve fully concurrent coordination of base translation, yaw, torso pitch, arm joints, and the gripper.
Even without expensive force/torque sensors, combining a momentum residual observer with energy-tank-based passivity control provides safe and practical contact force rendering.
Open fixed-base VLA models like MolmoAct2 can be easily adapted to whole-body coordination tasks on quadruped mobile manipulators once an appropriate full-body action space is defined.
limitations: Base acceleration is not accounted for in contact force estimation, causing rapid base acceleration or deceleration to misclassify inertial forces as external contacts.

Evaluation of the autonomous policy remains limited to qualitative success validation; quantitative assessments of how force feedback impacts demonstration quality or how success rates scale with data volume have not yet been conducted.
In extreme cases where the target moves into camera blind spots or the base stops with a large positioning offset, navigation failures can occur.
